England.difference_en: England begins comparing and ordering simple fractions in Year 3 and later uses equivalence, common denominators and benchmarks. Revised PEP introduces fractions in Grade 3 upper and develops formal fraction relationships in Grade 5 lower.
England.why_en: Fraction comparison depends on the fraction unit and the whole; numerator and denominator cannot be compared independently as whole numbers.
England.classroom_use_en: Compare 1/4 and 1/8 using the same whole, then compare 3/4 and 5/8 on a number line.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 3 treats fractions as numbers and compares fractions with the same numerator or denominator; Grade 4 extends to more general comparison.
US.why_en: The standards require comparison to be justified with models, benchmarks or equivalent fractions rather than symbols alone.
US.classroom_use_en: After comparing, require a number-line or benchmark explanation using 1/2 or 1.

England.difference_en: England Year 5 explicitly converts between improper fractions and mixed numbers and uses both forms in calculation. Revised PEP Grade 5 lower develops proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers within the fraction unit.
England.why_en: Locating an improper fraction beyond 1 on a number line gives the notation a quantity meaning before conversion rules are used.
England.classroom_use_en: Place 7/4 on a number line first, then explain why it is 1 3/4.

US.difference_en: Common Core elementary fraction standards use fractions greater than 1 and fraction operations, but mixed-number conversion is not organised as the same standalone progression seen in England.
US.why_en: The comparison should reflect the actual standards rather than treating different notation choices as missing concepts.
US.classroom_use_en: Establish the location of 7/4 on a number line, then connect it to mixed-number notation when useful.

England.difference_en: England starts with simple same-denominator fraction addition/subtraction in Year 3 and progresses to unlike denominators in Years 5-6. Revised PEP Grade 5 lower has a dedicated Fractions Addition and Subtraction unit.
England.why_en: Unlike-denominator operations require a common fraction unit; common denominators are not only a procedural step.
England.classroom_use_en: Use 1/3+1/4 to show why different-sized fraction units cannot be combined directly, then express both in twelfths.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 4 works with fraction-unit composition and same-denominator operations; Grade 5 formally adds and subtracts unlike-denominator fractions.
US.why_en: The progression moves from reasoning with fraction units to using equivalent fractions to create a common unit.
US.classroom_use_en: Before finding a common denominator, ask pupils to name the current unit in each fraction.

England.difference_en: England Year 5 begins with fractions multiplied by whole numbers; Year 6 extends to simple fraction-by-fraction multiplication. Revised PEP Grade 6 upper includes a dedicated Fractions Multiplication unit.
England.why_en: Fraction multiplication can be interpreted as scaling or taking a fraction of a quantity, so multiplication does not always make a number larger.
England.classroom_use_en: Compare 8×3/4, 8×1 and 8×5/4; predict relative size before calculating.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 5 systematically develops fraction multiplication and interprets it through scaling and visual models such as area.
US.why_en: This directly challenges the whole-number generalisation that multiplication always increases a quantity.
US.classroom_use_en: Predict whether multiplying by a number less than, equal to or greater than 1 will decrease, preserve or increase the original quantity.

England.difference_en: England Year 6 formally includes fractions divided by whole numbers, but does not require the same systematic fraction-by-fraction division progression as Common Core Grade 6. Revised PEP Grade 6 upper includes a dedicated Fractions Division unit.
England.why_en: This is a real difference in curriculum depth and organisation and should not be forced into same-grade equivalence.
England.classroom_use_en: Use a question such as 'How many one-halves are in 3?' to establish division meaning before deciding how far to extend the procedure.

US.difference_en: Common Core Grade 6 explicitly requires interpreting and computing quotients of fractions divided by fractions and solving related word problems.
US.why_en: Measurement/grouping interpretations give the quotient meaning before an invert-and-multiply algorithm is used.
US.classroom_use_en: Use a number line or bar model to answer how many groups of a fractional size fit into a quantity before applying the algorithm.
